pages.title: Credits
text: Tempo Trauma: an original game inspired by Trauma Center: Second Opinion (Atlus). Its world, cast, story, strains, gifts and art are new.
Engine: Pavilion (the shardfall repository, commit 49ef2ba), written in Rust. Renderer wgpu; menus egui; windowing winit; controllers gilrs; sound cpal and Web Audio; physics rapier.
Font: Barlow Condensed SemiBold, by the Barlow Project Authors (Jeremy Tribby), licensed under the SIL Open Font License 1.1.
Multiplayer: the AI Hub Session Protocol v1 client (session.js 1.4.0).
Everything else, including all music, sound effects and voices, is generated in code. No image, model or audio files.
Written and built by Claude (Anthropic, claude-sonnet-5-5, reasoning effort medium) through Claude Code. Usage: added on import

pages.title: Source Information
text: Source: Trauma Center: Second Opinion (Atlus, 2006)
Plan: PLAN.md (Game plan: an original surgical-action drama on the Pavilion engine)

Genre and Perspective: Surgical action (pointer-precision arcade game under a ticking clock) framed by a visual-novel medical melodrama, with drop-in co-op; Operations: a fixed surgeon's-eye view looking down at the operative field (73 degrees, mild perspective, short camera pushes); story: a staged paper theatre seen straight on

Tech: Pavilion engine (shardfall repo, commit 49ef2ba) in Rust 1.98.1: wgpu renderer, egui 0.36 shell, winit, gilrs, cpal and a code-written Web Audio synth; wasm-bindgen 0.2.129 to a single HTML file; AI Hub session protocol client 1.4.0

Art Direction: The engine's native cel-shaded style with ink outlines and bloom: a per-frame vertex-painted operative field, SDF instruments and parasites, and layered extruded spline cards for the paper-theatre story

Animation: The engine's sim-driven procedural animation: tool squeeze, cut and recoil, tissue pulse, creeping tendrils, swelling sacs, nodules stepping on the beat, and paper rigs that blink, breathe, sway and flap their mouths
Audio: All in code: about 35 synthesized sound cues, a heartbeat-following note sequencer with ten tracks, and Animalese-style voices (formant blips per syllable); music defaults to 10% volume
Online: AI Hub shared-world Code Blue round for 1-4 players (host-authoritative, 15 Hz snapshots and inputs, own pre-op card); the game runs fully on its own outside a session

Testing: Headless only: Rust tests (bot wins on 10 seeds, careless player loses, determinism, coverage, content lint, shell, audio) behind one command; Playwright browser tests on the built file with a stubbed DualSense, keyboard and mouse, phone profile and the AI Hub harness; screenshots only for visuals

Research: Research done by the plan: Trauma Center: Second Opinion (Atlus, Wii launch title, 2006), a remake of the DS Under the Knife; Wii Remote pointer and Nunchuk tool flick, two doctors with different gifts, day-named strains, rank scoring. No further research
Environment: Claude Code CLI (headless); Linux
Model: Anthropic, claude-sonnet-5-5, reasoning effort medium
Usage: added on import

pages.title: Testing Feedback
text: How many issues did testing catch?

Twelve real defects: a forceps grab that never fired when the trigger was already held, an Echo repeat that invalidated an index and panicked, an unreachable Case 7 nodule (the Scanner slot becomes the Cryoprobe there), a tendril the bot could not pull far enough, an idle player that won Case 7 through the partner bot, a story script under the plan's length, par values that left the bot at rank B, lost menu key taps between slow frames, a test hook that sent the wrong screen command, a Case Files jump that skipped the chart card, hub clients that stayed silent until play began, and a late ready() call.
How many would be considered critical issues / game breaking?

Five: the covered-hook grab that soft-locked Case 0, the Echo panic, the unreachable Case 7 nodule, the tendril that could not be finished (Case 4 could never be won), and the silent hub clients (the hub's own check fails a game that does not talk both ways).
What was the most helpful test you ran?

The headless scripted playthrough of the whole campaign (the bot plays every case and every story scene on ten seeds) plus the coverage counters: they found rule bugs in seconds and proved every tool, hazard, strain, gift and Code fires.
What was the least helpful test you ran?
Pixel screenshots of the operative field: useful for the look, but they said little about whether the rules worked, and each cost a build.

pages.title: Engine Feedback
text: What did you like most about the engine?

Everything runs headless: the same Sim, bot and capture tools drive tests, balance and screenshots, and the snapshot, rewind and replay hashes made determinism cheap to prove. The single-file web packer worked first time.
Did you get stuck or guess wrong?

Yes. I guessed the egui painter API (0.36 changed run_ui and content_rect), where gilrs keeps analog trigger values, and how the hook's input frame accumulates pressed bits (it only clears its own). The packer silently allows nothing outside the page, so wasm-bindgen snippets are a trap.
What was the most important thing you had to build yourself?

A separate product frame path: the engine's App::frame is the Shardfall demo, so the shell, input, camera, audio director and hub bridge for this game live in product.rs, hook.rs and the pav_ui surgery shell.
What was the hardest part about using the engine?

Memory. The workspace needs several GB per rustc and another agent's build on the same machine got mine killed repeatedly; and the lack of a per-game camera, input and renderer seam, which meant touching frame.rs, input.rs, build.rs, simhost.rs and the app.
What did you change in the engine, and why? (none if nothing)

Added SimEvent::Cue, SurgeonInput and SurgeryCmd on InputFrame, RenderFrame.surgery, a surgery view early-return in ViewBuilder::build, three audio buses with a band-pass formant filter and a music sequencer in pav_audio, a product frame path in pav_app, a session client, tags and shim in the packer, and the game's own mod under games/surgery.
If you could change one thing about the engine, what would it be?
A real per-game seam: a trait for a game's own frame, camera, input device map and UI, so a game does not fork App::frame.

pages.title: Prompt Feedback
text: What did you like most about this prompt?
The plan: it decided what mattered, marked what had been tested, and named every engine seam up front, so I spent my effort building rather than deciding.
What was confusing?

Little was confusing, but the scale was: the plan asks for a whole studio's output (a sim, a view, a theatre, a shell, an audio engine, a hub round, tests and a designer guide) in one sitting, and its own cut list is the only guide to what to drop.
What was the hardest thing to do?

Keeping many large systems consistent: one frame struct feeding the view, the shell, the audio director, the tests and the network mirror, and not breaking the other layers while a single-file build takes minutes on a shared, memory-starved machine.
What would you change in this prompt?
State the budget (hours or tokens) next to the scope, and give the whole-game vertical slice a ranked must-have list so the least important features can be cut first without guessing.
